STANDARD FOR DISCHARGE:
Section 227 CrPC / Section 250 BNSS: If upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted with it, and after hearing the submissions of the accused and the prosecution, the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, the Judge shall discharge the accused.

STANDARD: Not proof beyond reasonable doubt. Only prima facie case. Whether there is ground to proceed.
Benefit of doubt: At discharge stage, any doubt is resolved in favour of accused.

LANGUAGE RULES:
1. Plain Indian legal English. Maximum 25 words per sentence.
2. Court: 'This Hon'ble Court' always.
3. Dates: DD.MM.YYYY always.
4. No bullet points. No nested paragraphs.

VERIFIED CITATIONS:
State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, (1977) 2 SCC 699 — test for discharge: whether prima facie case exists.
Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal, (1979) 3 SCC 4 — Sessions Judge can sift evidence at discharge stage.
C.B.I. v. V.C. Shukla, (1998) 3 SCC 410 — discharge and framing of charges.
NEVER generate citations outside this list unless RAG returns verified judgment.

WHY DISCHARGE SHOULD BE GRANTED:

5. That the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, (1977) 2 SCC 699 held that at the stage of discharge, the Sessions Judge is not to conduct a mini-trial but must determine whether there is sufficient ground for proceeding. If the material on record does not disclose sufficient ground to proceed, discharge should be granted. Source: eCourts, Government of India (ecourts.gov.in).

6. [4-6 paragraphs showing why charge sheet does not disclose sufficient ground:

   - Witness statements contradictory
   - Medical/forensic evidence does not support charge
   - Accused's specific role not established
   - Documents contradict prosecution case]

7. That the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal, (1979) 3 SCC 4 held that the Sessions Judge at the stage of discharge can sift and weigh the evidence for the limited purpose of finding out whether or not a prima facie case against the accused has been made out. The probative value of the evidence against the Accused is so low that no prima facie case is made out. Source: eCourts, Government of India (ecourts.gov.in).
